thread: The contamination is built: a layered, craft-made substance in a jar (and Jaina's awe and fear)

evidence.clue: Under a loft floorboard: a clay round-bellied jar the size of a baby's head with waxed cloth over the mouth; broken, it spills a dark substance darker than oil that runs along the grain of the boards in 'thin dark fingers' toward the hole, the open sack and Sylvanas's boots; smells of pears gone brown and, under it, a struck flint.

Jaina's blue shell ward over the spill holds: 'a bowl dropped over a candle'; the stuff lies black and still under it with a skin forming 'cooling jam'. She reads it: the same thing as in Garran, the doe's blood, the Millhaven well (the same late drag), but whole: 'It had been built.' A stack of spells laid on each other 'planking on a hull, every seam caulked': one part to keep, one part to wait, one part she cannot follow; it went into flour, through an oven, into a man's milk, 'and sat down in him and waited'.

She recognises it as the death-currents craft that makes a corpse get up and walk: Kirin Tor apprentices are walked past the locked shelf in their first year and given the signs so they will know it, never the grammar (it 'stayed behind the grille'). 'This was written in the grammar. She could read every letter of it and not one word.' She thinks it beautiful and wants to take it apart.
Aloud: 'It's made. Somebody very good made this.'
The shell held until first light. Brask had the loft boards carried down flat with Jaina's ice on them and burned with the rest. The jar's contents and the third part are destroyed unread.
Jaina ties the build to Antonidas's standards: 'Whoever had made this had made it as Antonidas built a ward.'

Chapter 6, opening: the same late, dragging hitch comes up through the mare and staff on every bend of the south road and matches what Jaina felt at Millhaven with the staff heel in a dead man's print. She fits the evidence together: the young man with the cart, Corley's book of loads, Sylvanas's slips with Andorhal at one end, Garran's bread sops twice a day all summer, the jar 'made to keep and made to wait', and Millhaven's dead walking north on the cow way. Bad luck (wet harvest, mould, fever sharing wells) and 'one clever man with a cart and a grudge' are ruled out: a fever does not come in layers a fortnight apart or keep to one road; one man could not have driven every load and swept the depot floor and stuffed the stove and kept the overseer's answers ready and stitched paper into a boy's collar.

Chapter 6: the model stated: 'It was one thing, made in parts, every part with a job: the carts to carry it, the mills and bakehouses to put it into bread, the people to eat it a little at a time. The jar's keeping part kept it whole inside them, and it built there meal after meal and waited. When enough of it had gathered in them, they died, and then their bodies got up and walked.' Aloud: 'It comes in on the wagons and walks out on its own feet.'

Chapter 6: the missing step: Jaina cannot say 'how it gets from a knot under a man's breastbone to his feet walking after he's dead. That's the part of the jar I couldn't read.' She wonders what kind of keeping could survive a mill, an oven and a gut: 'past anything she'd been taught or made.'

Chapter 6: the fear. A master in her first year told the room under the locked grille that the whole of that art came down to keeping a body useful after the person in it had gone, which was why the grille was locked. The design is laid out as she was taught to lay a ward (every seam closed, nothing loose for the next spell to catch on): 'Whoever had built this had been taught in Dalaran.' She runs down faces (masters, senior students, ones who left and never wrote) and stops at one; no name. She wants the whole road on a bench under a good lamp; she calls it study, a piece of work looked at properly for Antonidas, and wants to see the keeping part work once. Her body answers with nausea and sour spit.

Chapter 7 (Jaina's report): the sample-room bags on copied marks read 'heavy', on true marks 'clean'. The poison is a coat too thin to see, put on by hand after the grain is dressed and before the sack is sewn, worked through so every grain gets some. On its own the coat does little; what it carries wakes once the bread is eaten, inside whoever ate it. Whoever filled the crock 'knows his way round an alchemist's bench, and necromancy. Both.'

Chapter 7 (Sylvanas's sighting): at Kett's, five masked men in waxed cloths and long gloves work a dark thick substance from a crock into open sacks with the arm buried to the elbow, sew them shut, stack them; gloves come off without touching skin and go into a bucket, forearms are washed, the cloth lowered only to drink. The masked men protect themselves from the grain, not from dust. Jaina: 'Whatever's on the outside of those gloves can kill the man inside them.'
Chapter 7: the loft is 'wet' tonight (gloves, bucket, floor round the crock); Jaina can still read the residue there and will not once the gloves are burned and the boards swilled.

readerKnows_chapter7: The carrier layer is applied at packaging by skilled alchemical and necromantic hands under self-protection; the body finishes the work. The handling cell is organised and disciplined. Who designed the process and how a victim becomes undead after death are still unknown. (Ch7-8 rung only: no answering chamber, no fidelity talk, no source named.)
povCharacterKnows_chapter7: Sylvanas and Jaina: the coat is hand-applied at Kett's with protective gear; what is in the crock is unknown; the next step is a living prisoner.
readerKnows_chapter6: The plague is one distributed system built by trained hands: carts, mills and bakehouses, the keeping part inside the body, death, then walking. Jaina's private fear points at a Dalaran-trained author and a face she will not name. Sylvanas knows the model only as Jaina says it aloud; the missing step remains missing.
povCharacterKnows_chapter6: Jaina: the system, the Dalaran signature, the gap in how sickness becomes walking; a fear with no name. Sylvanas: the model, the 'somebody with training', no name. Arthas: told it and believed it as far as he could see it. No character names Kel'Thuzad or Mal'Ganis.
notes_chapter6: Plan guard held: no Mal'Ganis naming, no Kel'Thuzad naming, no 'answering chamber' model or low/high fidelity (Ch9-12). Ladder: ingestion, repeated exposure, body participation isolated; death completes it only in Jaina's closing sentence of the model, not explained.
readerKnows: The contamination is deliberate craft in a necromantic grammar the Kirin Tor withhold; it has a keeping part, a waiting part and an unreadable third; it can be stored in jars and carried in flour.
povCharacterKnows: Jaina: she can describe the shape and feel the seams but cannot read the third part; the Kirin Tor apprentice syllabus acknowledges it but does not teach it. Sylvanas: knows only what Jaina says.
notes: Source: the maker is unknown. Do not give the maker's name or school yet. Jaina's awe is a character beat: she may want to understand it (a danger). 'Death-currents' craft is named only in her interior as common Dalaran first-year knowledge; this is not a revelation of Jaina's ignorance.
